title: Witold Pilecki — the man who got himself sent to Auschwitz
sources: Wikipedia: Witold Pilecki (13 May 1901 – 25 May 1948) — Polish cavalry officer and resistance leader, co-founder of the Secret Polish Army; little was known about the new Auschwitz camp; it was proposed that he infiltrate it, presented as an invitation to volunteer, and he agreed; arrested on 19 September 1940 under the identity of Tomasz Serafiński, either in a Warsaw street round-up or during a building search (two versions exist); reached Auschwitz on 21–22 September 1940 as prisoner 4859; survived slave-labour details and pneumonia; organised the underground ZOW in secret five-man cells that eventually included hundreds of inmates; smuggled reports out with released or escaped inmates; built a radio transmitter from smuggled parts over seven months; his information was a principal source of intelligence on Auschwitz for the Western Allies; hoped for an Allied or Home Army attack on the camp, which never came; on the night of 26–27 April 1943 escaped through a bakery door outside the fence with two comrades; shot at and wounded while fleeing; fought in the Warsaw Uprising of 1944; after the war returned to communist Poland to report for the government-in-exile; arrested 8 May 1947, tortured, revealed nothing; show trial in March 1948; executed with a shot to the back of the head at Mokotów Prison on 25 May 1948; burial place never found; his story was suppressed by the communist authorities for decades

Photos (public domain, Wikimedia Commons): Pilecki as an officer; his Auschwitz prisoner photographs (no. 4859, 1940); his prison photographs (1947); at his trial (1948); the execution record (1948); the Auschwitz gate and camp at liberation, 1945 (Soviet photographers); the Warsaw Uprising, 1944
Archive film (public domain): 'Auschwitz (Oświęcim) Reel 1' (Soviet liberation film, 1945) — the camp as found in January 1945
Music: Chopin, Marche funèbre — Paul Pitman for Musopen, public domain

post.facebook:
In 1940, one man got himself arrested — so the Germans would send him to Auschwitz.

Witold Pilecki was a Polish cavalry officer in the resistance. Nobody knew what was really happening inside the new camp, and a volunteer was needed. He said yes. He let the Germans catch him in Warsaw under a false name, and days later he was prisoner 4859.

He survived slave labour and pneumonia — and built a secret army inside, in cells of five. His men smuggled out reports of the killings and even built a radio from smuggled parts. His reports became a main source on Auschwitz for the Allies. He hoped for an attack to free the camp. It never came.

In April 1943, after two and a half years inside, he broke out through a bakery door. Shot at and wounded, he made it back to the resistance, and a year later fought in the Warsaw Uprising.

After the war, Poland fell under communist rule. Pilecki stayed. In 1947 the secret police caught him and tortured him; he gave up no one. After a show trial he was shot in the back of the head. His grave has never been found.

He walked into Auschwitz by choice, and came out alive. It was his own country that killed him.

🇵🇱 #History #WW2 #Pilecki #Auschwitz

youtube.description:
In 1940, one man got himself arrested, so the Germans would send him to Auschwitz.

Witold Pilecki, a Polish resistance officer, entered Auschwitz under a false name as prisoner 4859, built a secret underground army inside, smuggled out reports that became a main source on the camp for the Allies, and escaped in April 1943. He fought in the Warsaw Uprising — and in 1948 was executed after a show trial by communist Poland. His grave has never been found.
